conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You were admitted today because of left groin and lower abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what you're feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. The pain started last night around midnight. It’s a cramping, tight feeling in my left groin and lower belly. It feels like a muscle spasm, but pain meds aren’t helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You mentioned this feels similar to something you had a month ago?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Last time, they found swollen lymph nodes on ultrasound. But this pain is worse and hasn’t gone away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you haven’t passed gas since the pain started?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not since it began. I’m a bit worried it might be a blockage or something serious.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a valid concern. We did a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis earlier. It didn’t show any bowel obstruction or acute surgical issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s some soft tissue inflammation in your left groin area. Also, the known mass near your bladder — which we know is related to your myeloma — hasn’t changed in size.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you think the pain is from the myeloma mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s our leading thought. The inflammation in the groin could be due to a plasmacytoma — a tumor from your plasma cells — pressing on nerves or tissues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time they gave me steroids and it helped. Could that work again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re going to start you on dexamethasone, a steroid, to reduce inflammation. It often helps with this kind of pain in myeloma patients.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But I’m also on Revlimid and Ninlaro — should I keep taking those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your Revlimid and Ninlaro soon. You just had chemo yesterday, so we’re making sure your counts are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood counts are always low. I’ve been neutropenic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white count is low at 2.6, and your neutrophils are very low — only 0.49. That’s why we’re being cautious with restarting treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my platelets? I’ve had issues with bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your platelets are 43, which is low but not critically so. We’ll monitor them closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidney function? My creatinine has been up and down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.6 today. It’s been fluctuating — sometimes as low as 1.1, now around 1.5–1.7. It could be due to your myeloma or diabetes. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Actually, it’s a bit better since I got the steroid yesterday. Still there, but not as intense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s encouraging. We’re going to continue the dexamethasone. We also met with radiation oncology — they’ll see you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Radiation? For the mass?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. They plan to treat the area near your bladder with radiation to shrink the plasmacytoma and help with pain control long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How many treatments will I need?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re planning 14 outpatient sessions. The first one is scheduled for tomorrow at 1 PM.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. And my myeloma meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re restarting Revlimid today. Ninlaro will follow as planned. We’ll continue monitoring your blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming — you took your Revlimid dose this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I did. No nausea or other side effects so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Your liver enzymes are slightly elevated — AST 52, ALT 67. Likely from the steroid burst, but we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before with steroids. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level. It’s mild and likely temporary. We’ll check again before discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your pain now, Mr. ___?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I still feel some pressure, but the cramping is gone. I’m sleeping better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Your labs this morning show your hemoglobin is stable at 7.4, platelets down to 22, but no bleeding. Neutrophil count improved to 1.49.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Platelets are dropping. Should I avoid certain activities?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just be cautious — avoid heavy lifting or anything that could cause bruising. We’re not planning transfusions unless you develop symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my diabetes — I know steroids can spike my sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your glucose was 162 this morning — elevated but not critical. We’re stopping the steroids soon and restarting your home insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on glargine at night. I’ll need my sliding scale back too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll have that ready. Your A1C was 8.6 last check — we’ll follow up with endocrinology if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news — you’re being discharged today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What’s the plan now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll start radiation therapy today at 1 PM. 14 treatments total. Continue your Revlimid and Ninlaro as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oxycodone for breakthrough pain. Use as needed. Also, keep taking your other regular meds — we’ve updated your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll follow up with my oncologist?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and with your primary doctor for blood counts and kidney function. Call us if pain worsens or you develop fever or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad the steroid helped. Take care, and good luck with radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll wait for them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — your creatinine is 1.5 today. Keep hydrated and monitor for swelling or fatigue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. I know my kidneys have been shaky.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll schedule a follow-up blood test in a week. Take it easy, and we’ll see how you do with radiation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Appreciate all the help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your oncology team about your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I feel confident with the plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. See you soon.
